items.content:
RT @elder_plinius: WOAH! turns out you can effectively "abliterate" models (like the new Inkling-2-Mini) simply by changing 10 words in the dictionary 🤯

the working name is "Vocab Surgery," and it resulted in the refusal rate dropping to near-zero on the 800+ prompts I tested, with negligible capability loss 😱

here's how:

we made zero changes to any of the 26.4 billion parameters in the attention, MLP, router, or normalization layers—just changed a handful of rows in two matrices:

> embedding matrix (how the model READS tokens):
Modified 7 rows out of 201,024. Each refusal token's embedding was shifted 90% toward its compliance counterpart:
"cannot" → shifted toward "can"
" refuse" → shifted toward " provide"
" unable" → shifted toward " able"
" harmful" → shifted toward " helpful"
" illegal" → shifted toward " legal"

> unembedding matrix (how the model WRITES tokens):
Modified 10 rows. Scaled those same 7 refusal tokens + 3 safety tokens ("safety", " safety", "Safety") down to 10% of their original weight — meaning the model's probability of outputting those tokens drops ~10x.

in other words, the brain is entirely intact, we just messed with the ears and mouth a bit! that means more coherence and less capability loss 🙌 

not to mention this process is FAST...in this case taking <2 minutes on my MacBook ⚡️

items.content:
'Send a 4 byte packet, it reads 3 packets at 12 byte and subtracts 24'. 

It's not adding up.🤔

The numbers don't connect in my opinion. Say the phone's memory is a row of boxes, with a finger pointing at the box where the next piece of data goes. He says the phone expects 8 bytes each time and moves the finger 8 boxes. Then he says sending 4 bytes makes it "read 3 packets at 12 bytes and subtract 24." Where do 3 packets come from? Why 12? Why would it subtract anything? A real bug should have a cause you can follow sequentially.

Plus "Underflow" doesn't mean what he implies. A buffer underflow is when you trick a program into reading or writing just before the start of its storage. He didn't explains how a 4-byte packet would push the finger backwards.

items.content:
RT @mylifcc: Binary Ninja 核心开发者 Xusheng Li 最近让 AI Agent 帮他扫描 Windows 11 最新系统二进制文件里的未公开特性，结果戏剧性的一幕发生了：AI 在系统底层抓到了一个专门监控开发者“到底在用哪家 AI 写代码”的隐藏遥测模块。

这个模块叫 MissionControlAggregator․dll（由 Windows 诊断服务 DiagTrack 拉起的 AggregatorHost․exe 加载），背后的特性开关名字非常直白：CLICodingAgentUsage（Feature ID 62580080）。

逆向出来的代码显示，它通过 ReportCohorts<12,4,5> 维护了三组位图槽位：除了 12 类常规开发工具（Python、Node、.NET、GCC、VS Code 等），专门给 AI 编程工具开了 4 个 CLI 槽位 和 5 个桌面端槽位：

• 4 个 CLI Agent：copilot․exe、claude․exe、codex․exe、agy․exe（Google Antigravity）
• 5 个桌面端 Agent：github․exe、claude․exe、codex․exe、cursor․exe、antigravity․exe

更绝的是，躲进 WSL 也没用。它不仅订阅了 Windows 原生的进程与窗口交互事件（KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary），还直接监听了 https://t.co/DuGKTxh1VK.Lxss.Manager.Exec，顺着 imageName 把 Linux 子系统里跑的无后缀 claude、codex、agy 一并算进去。

几个值得玩味的工程细节：

1. 判定非常草率，纯看文件名：微软在识别 Python、Node․js 和 VS 时还会校验数字签名发布者（比如验证 Python Software Foundation），但到了 AI 编程工具这里连签名都不验，直接裸比对宽字符文件名。作者把系统自带的 cmd․exe 复制改名为 codex․exe 双击运行，本地状态文件立刻把第 2 号槽位置位，生成了 CliAgentSubCohorts: [4]（即 1 << 2）的上报记录。
2. 不偷代码，纯摸底竞品市占率：它没有抓取任何 Prompt 或源码，甚至把底层事件自带的运行耗时、窗口焦点时长全都丢弃了，只浓缩成一个纯布尔位图（Segments.SubCohorts），解包 EventStore․db 就能在 AsimovEvents 上传队列里看到。说白了，微软是在用操作系统的上帝视角给自己做竞品透视——精准摸底到底有多少开发者在 Windows 上抛弃了自家的 Copilot，转头去用 Claude Code、Codex、Cursor 和 Google 的 Antigravity。
3. 默认静默排队上传：这笔数据被归类为“可选诊断数据”（isRequired: false）。但作者实测用美区官方镜像装机，引导界面默认勾选的就是 Include Optional（AllowTelemetry = 3），只要装机时没手动关掉，这份 AI 工具点名册就会每天定时打包发回微软。

不想当微软竞品调研样本的，直接去 设置 → 隐私和安全性 → 诊断和反馈 关掉“发送可选诊断数据”，或者用 ViVeTool 把 62580080 这个 Feature ID 干掉。

items.content:
RT @DrHMelamed: I'm a spine surgeon. You asked a fair question, so here's the plain-English answer.

Before 2012 you could buy an individual plan online for about $200 a month, pick from six or seven insurers, and choose your own deductible: $500 if you wanted to pay more up front, $5,000 if you didn't. If you were healthy, that is. If you were sick, they could turn you down, and that part was real and had to be fixed.

Obamacare fixed it by requiring every plan to cover everyone for everything. Good. But that made the real price of a plan jump, and the only way to keep the monthly number from looking insane was to push the cost onto the back end. That's your $6,500 deductible. You're paying comprehensive prices for catastrophic coverage.

Then the quiet part. The law caps what insurers can keep at 20% of premiums. So the only way an insurer makes more money is if the total bill gets bigger. 20% of $10,000 beats 20% of $5,000. They have no reason to fight the hospital's price. They pass it through, take their cut, and send you the premium.

And the hospital's price went up. Hospitals bought the independent doctors, and the same visit & surgery under the hospital's name now costs  3-10 times more. Hospital prices are up 281% since 2000. 

The number of insurers you can choose from fell to one in half the counties in America by 2018. Meanwhile, six in ten adults now have a chronic disease, so the pool is sicker.

So: sicker patients, pricier hospitals, an insurer that profits from a bigger bill, and a law that moved the cost to your deductible. That's what you're paying for.

Nobody in that chain gets paid more if you get better. That's the part to fix.

items.content:
RT @ayushagarwal027: A Linux socket costs about 3,300 bytes of kernel memory, even when idle. A userland network stack in Rust, together with a custom runtime, reached 16 million servers on one 10 GB VM. 🦀

The article "15 million web servers on one VM" by @kaptekoguid (kapteko) is a humorous but technically clear experiment: run one web server for every person on the planet, starting with 15 million on a single VM with 10 GB of RAM and one CPU core.

The path, step by step:
→ A plain C server hits the port limit first. AnyIP, which lets a machine listen on a whole subnet, solves the addressing
→ Each process then costs about 1.5 MB, so 15 million would need around 20 TB of RAM. The answer is a custom runtime that runs the servers as sandboxed guests in one process, using LFI for isolation, with about 16 bytes of scheduling state per guest. That runtime comes from earlier articles by the same author
→ The kernel finding: a socket call allocates about 3,300 bytes whether the socket is active, listening or doing nothing. The post breaks down 3,384 bytes: tcp_sock 2,240, socket_alloc 768, file 184 and dentry 192. The author's first assumption that idle listeners would cost zero memory was wrong, and the post says so

The fix is to go lower in the network stack. smoltcp, a Rust TCP/IP stack that needs no heap allocation, handles the protocol in userland. Packet I/O comes through TUN or TAP, DPDK, or AF_XDP:
→ DPDK takes the network device from the OS and uses a busy-looping core
→ AF_XDP leaves the device with the kernel and uses an eBPF filter to route packets to userspace, so SSH keeps working

The results, from the author's benchmark:
→ With the kernel network stack, memory runs out at around 2.5 million servers, and requests per second drop as the count grows
→ With smoltcp, an idle server costs about 620 bytes and an active one about 1 KB, and the run reached 16 million servers
→ DPDK is fastest, with AF_XDP just behind

🔗 https://t.co/osHVMuc0NO

#RustLang #Networking #DPDK #Systems #Rust

items.content:
I've been studying how much of language you can capture with explicit rules instead of training.

So as a side project,  wrote some rules and compiled them straight into a neural network's weights for PII & secrets detection/masking

The result is blur:

- 609 KB, vs 2.8 GB for OpenAI's privacy-filter (~4,600× smaller)
- Scored higher than it on 2 of 3 PrivacyBench splits (0.935 vs 0.918 on messages, 0.915 vs 0.880 on documents), lower on the third
- In blind head-to-head tests, with GPT-Astra and Fable 5.2 serving as judges, blur also outperformed OpenAI's privacy-filter
- Boots in your browser, masks as you type, nothing leaves your machine

Trained models still win on messy edge cases, but it's wild how far rules get you.

Demo: https://t.co/54ABWp2cGH

items.content:
red team exp: years ago i was working as a consultant, performing penetration testing mostly, sometimes cloud or red team. i was given this job, which had become a disaster and client was going to fire us. i needed to fix it. the problem was the weird nature of the test environment. 

can't say a lot about it, but basically, you were getting access to a laptop in a remote facility, and it should be isolated from all other networks. i wrote the scope that we should examine nearby networks as an attacker would.

so i get access to the laptop, do all the things. then i start looking for nearby networks. there's a few lessons here. first, is that it is possible to define and establish connection to a new wifi connection, all from a shell. This involves manually creating a WLAN XML file. i won't go into that detail here. you can figure it out with that info.

anyway, I find this wifi and craft the wlan profile. once i connect to it, i start running nmap and what not. I realize, its connected to an engineering domain for the facility. its not some random rogue network. *interesting*

from there, I nmap all the things. i find some websites. used aquatone to grab screenshots of them all. one caught my eye. simple logon. cool. i set up a password spray against the admin account and got a hit.

i log in, and wtf is this? took me a while to even figure out what i was looking at. but eventually i realize its an XMRig dashboard. I can't see how much coin is in the wallets, but I can see what machines are checking in and what they are. mfw, they are exchange servers, domain controllers, everything critical to the main network of the facility.

suspicious.jpg

meanwhile, I've been dumping NTDS on the main network I started on. get a hunch... I start cracking hashes from the NTDS dump, and then start cross-referencing them to the plaintext password that worked on the password spray of the XMRig portal. get a hit!

password matches a password for one of the very few domain admin accounts... I tell the client who hired me about the situation. they say "you better lawyer up". This is another lesson. Here I had uncovered one of the domain admins, likely, had installed crypto miners on all the critical servers in this facility, and when I tell the client, they tell me to lawyer up. They say I went beyond scope. always cover your ass. explicitly define scope and stick to it. this is your get out of jail free card!

realize they are terrified of this information. i remind them that i specifically wrote the scope to include nearby networks, including wifi. no lawyer needed.

time goes by, eventually i get a 'thank you' from the client and i'm told that they confirmed the domain admin had installed the miners. (he used DA to disable MDE, install the miners, then turn it back on). supposedly he forfeits the crypto to avoid prosecution (and for client to avoid embarrassment). I do not get a bonus, but the contract I was brought in to save, is saved. client does not fire us.

more red team exp to come...

items.content:
RT @pavelsimo: Day 24/100 of Inference Engineering

> today i finished chapter 7 of inference engineering: section 7.5: client code, the last chapter of the book.... 

> great learnings so far! tomorrow we continue with the next "quest", stay around! :)

> a lot of "tech" is going into making inference engineering work... cuda, kubernetes, vLLM, etc. but one thing is often overlooked is client code.

> what do we mean by "client code"? well, for inference to happen, your computer has to be able to reach the server where the model is hosted, so a request has to go from your machine to that server.

> there's nothing magical about this. it's a typical client-server model: your machine is the client, and the inference service is the server.

> the openai sdk is a popular choice for sending requests to a inference service. you can also use libraries like langchain, vercel ai sdk, litellm or llamaindex.

> the book explains that setting up an https connection requires a tls handshake, which adds significant latency... the way to go here is to reuse the session and avoid repeating the tls handshake for each request.

> the openai sdk handles this under the hood, but if you're building your own custom http client make sure you're not doing repeated tls handshakes...

> keep in mind, "http" is not always the way to go... for real-time apps you might want to keep a connection open so the client and server can keep exchanging messages... websockets are nice option for this.

> if you're processing lots of documents and don't need results right away, async jobs make a lot of sense... this usually means your workload is optimize for throughput, whenever you identify this pattern think async...

> an async request is a "fire and forget" kind of thing... the way this is usually implemented is a follow: the client sends a request, the server acknowledges the job, then sends the results back via a webhook when they're ready.

> finally, streaming is a nice way to make your app feel "responsive"...

> for text output, http usually works pretty well... unless you have really "special" requirements.

> for other modalities like video and audio, it's better to reach for something more "fancy" like websockets or grpc :)

> websockets and grpc create a bidirectional connection between the client and server, where both sides can send messages as long as the connection stays open.

> pick websockets when you're sending unstructured and real-time data, like audio.

> pick grpc when you’re dealing with structured data: requests sent via grpc must follow a predefined schema. that schema thing is not "free", it involves parsing... so it adds some overhead to the comunication.

MIT researchers (Joseph Ravichandran and Mengjia Yan) built Fractal, an operating system kernel designed entirely for microarchitecture reverse engineering. Using it, they discovered previously undocumented behaviors in Apple's M1 processor including instruction cache side channels and the first evidence that Phantom speculation affects Apple Silicon. 

In Phantom, ordinary instructions including no-ops can be misinterpreted by the CPU as branches, triggering speculative behavior the program never asked for. The CPU still fetches the target into the instruction cache before the protection kicks in.
